newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Jan 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Jan 30.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Thursday's The Wall Street Journal:
* The auction of $7 billion of the U.S. Government's new 10-year, inflation-indexed bonds was oversubscribed, with investors seeking five times the amount offered.
* America Online reached a prelimary pact to pay up to $40 to customers who have had problems accessing the service since the company began flat-rate pricing in December.
* Ford Motor posted an 82 percent increase in fourth quarter profits on stronger results from its financial services and domestic auto operations.
* Countries including Canada and Mexico oppose the cross-border control of telephone companies that the United States and Europe are seeking as part of a world telecommunications pact.
* Mercury Finance said it found phony bookkeeping entries that led to overstate its 1996 profits by more than 100 percent and said company Controller James Doyle has disappeared.
* U.S. Treasury chief Robert Rubin prompted Internal Revenue Service Commissioner Margaret Richardson to submit her resignation, indicating Rubin is concerned about the condition of the tax agency.
* Durable goods orders fell 1.7 percent in December, reducing worries that the economy may be overheating.
* Bayer AG's U.S. unit pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges in the citric acid market and agrees to pay a $50 million fine.
* Magellan Health is expected to announce that it is divesting its 95 psychiatric hospitals in a pact with Crescent Real Estate Equities for about $400.
* Salomon Inc's Salomon Bros plans to seek SEC approval to offer options based on mutual-fund performance rather than stock prices.
* Hilton Hotels has not filed formal offer documents for its $6.5 billion bid for ITT Corp, which gives ITT time to prepare its defenses.
* Ford Motor reached a new settlement over litigation involving its Bronco II model and said it will help pay for certain work on the vehicles.
* Intel's price cuts on its most powerful computer chips are lower than expected, indicating that the California company believes it can move with little fear of competition.
* Samsung's U.S. unit joined other Korean chip makers in a pledge to cut their production of computer memory chips.
* Everyone knows following the herd on Wall Street can be a bad idea. Take the case of 3Com and Cascade Communications.

Both companies, which are in different segments of the super-hot computer-networking market, have gotten hammered in recent days as worries about a slowdown in their businesses have taken hold. -- Heard on the Street.

* The successful debut of "inflation-indexed" Treasury securities dominated an otherwise lackluster day for bonds yesterday and provided encouragement to a Treasury Department eager to gain investor acceptance for a new breed of U.S. government security designed to protect holders from inflation. -- Credit Markets.
